quote: and weak passwords in rsh
problem: Ch9 uses rsh as already known and says the Morris worm exploited 'weak passwords in rsh'. Ch10 is where rsh is first explained, as a command that logs listed hosts in 'without a password'. So rsh appears before it is explained, and the two chapters disagree about whether rsh uses passwords at all. Historically the worm abused rsh's passwordless trust between hosts and guessed weak passwords for rexec.
fix: ch9-security-p2: replace 'and weak passwords in `rsh`' with 'and the trust between machines that let `rsh` (remote login) skip the password for listed hosts, helped along by guessing weak passwords'. Optionally, in ch10-attacks-p7, write 'trusted `rsh`, the passwordless login the Morris worm abused (Chapter 9): on the assumption…'
reason: ch9-security-p2 uses rsh unexplained and as a password problem; ch10-attacks-p7 explains it as passwordless trust. The worm used rsh/rexec trust plus guessed passwords, so the two chapters read as disagreeing.
judge_fix: ch9-security-p2: replace 'and weak passwords in `rsh`' with 'and the trust between machines that let `rsh` (remote login) skip the password for listed hosts, helped by guessable passwords'. Leave ch10-attacks-p7.

quote: the same-origin policy, CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and more) were retrofitted over thirty years
problem: The chapter closer counts the same-origin policy among the defences 'retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked'. But ch12-security-p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say the policy shipped in Netscape 2.0, 'the same release that shipped JavaScript itself'. It came with the language, not after attacks.
fix: ch12-security-p10: 'The security mechanisms around it began with the same-origin policy, which shipped with the language itself; CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and the rest were retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked.'
reason: ch12-security-p10 lists the same-origin policy among defences 'retrofitted in response to attacks', but ch12-security-p2 and the Fig 12.8 strip say it shipped with JavaScript in Netscape 2.0.
judge_fix: ch12-security-p10: 'The security mechanisms that surround it began with the same-origin policy, which shipped with the language itself; CSRF tokens, Content Security Policy and the rest were retrofitted over thirty years in response to attacks that worked.'

quote: needs three of its primitives: hashing, symmetric encryption, and public-key cryptography
problem: The crypto briefing promises 'enough to read the TLS handshake'. But it only explains public-key encryption (the public key locks, the private key unlocks) and Diffie–Hellman. Section 05 then depends on digital signatures: 'The signature, made with the certificate's private key, proves the server…', and Fig 12's chain 'checks each signature with the public key of the certificate above it'. That is the reverse direction, and Part III never explains it. Chapter 14 is the first place that does.
fix: ch11-crypto-p7, after 'Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key.', insert: 'Run the other way, the pair gives a *signature*: the owner of the private key can sign a message, anyone holding the public key can check the signature, and nobody without the private key could have made it. That is how a server proves who it is (Section 05).'
reason: Section 04 promises enough to read the TLS handshake but never explains signatures; ch11-tls-p2, the Fig 11.11 strip and Fig 11.12 all rely on 'the signature proves the server holds the private key'. Part III has no explanation before this.
judge_fix: ch11-crypto-p7, after 'Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key.', insert: 'Run the other way, the pair makes a *signature*: only the owner of the private key can produce it, and anyone holding the public key can check it. That is how a server proves who it is (Section 05).'

quote: Each Finished is a MAC over the whole transcript, so tampering shows.
problem: The only 'MAC' Part III has taught is the 48-bit MAC address of Chapter 8. Here MAC means a message authentication code, which is never expanded. The prose in ch11-tls-p2 calls the same thing 'a hash of the entire transcript'. So one term has two meanings, and one object has two names.
fix: Fig 11.11 strip: 'Each Finished carries a keyed hash of the whole transcript, so tampering shows.'
reason: Fig 11.11 strip uses 'MAC' unexpanded; the only MAC taught in Part III is the Ethernet address (ch8). The prose in ch11-tls-p2 calls the same object 'a hash of the entire transcript'.
judge_fix: Fig 11.11 strip: 'Each Finished is a hash of the whole transcript, made with the new keys, so tampering shows.' Optionally ch11-tls-p2: 'carry a keyed hash of the entire transcript'.

quote: A forger never sees the reply, so it cannot hold a TCP conversation
problem: The Fig 9.10 strip says a forger cannot hold a TCP conversation. Chapter 10 then tells how Mitnick did exactly that: with a spoofed source, he predicted the ISN and blind-sent the ACK and a command. The Ch9 rule is stated as absolute and the Ch10 story breaks it. The same strip says the SYN flood 'relies on' spoofing, while ch10-attacks-p2 says 'often spoofed'.
fix: Fig 9.10 strip: 'One way only. A forger never sees the reply, so it can hold a TCP conversation only by guessing what the replies said (Chapter 10's Mitnick attack); spoofing suits single packets, which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood uses it.'
reason: Fig 9.10 strip states as absolute that a forger cannot hold a TCP conversation; ch10-attacks-p7 tells how Mitnick did it blind. The strip's 'relies on' for the SYN flood also clashes with ch10-attacks-p2 'often spoofed'.
judge_fix: Fig 9.10 strip: 'One way only. A forger never sees the reply, so it can hold a TCP conversation only by guessing what the replies say (Chapter 10's Mitnick attack); spoofing suits single packets, which is why Chapter 10's SYN flood often uses it.'

quote: QUIC (Quick UDP Internet Connections, RFC 9000, 2021) replaces TCP entirely for HTTP traffic.
problem: QUIC is introduced in full twice, and the second time it is presented as new. Both passages say it runs over UDP, rebuilds reliability, streams and congestion control, carries TLS 1.3 inside, and began at Google in 2012 before the 2021 IETF standard. Head-of-line blocking is also defined twice: in Ch10 as the TCP lost-packet stall, then in ch11-modern-p2 as the HTTP/1.1 slow-response queue. Neither passage refers to the other.
fix: ch10-modern-p6: replace the head-of-line parenthesis with 'Loss in one stream no longer stalls the others, a gain Chapter 11 shows in full (Fig 11.15).' ch11-modern-p5: open with 'QUIC, met in Chapter 10 (Section 05), was built for exactly this: each stream is ordered independently, so a lost packet on stream A no longer holds back stream B.' Then cut the repeated list of what it rebuilds and the 2012–2017 rollout history.
reason: QUIC (UDP, reliability/streams/congestion control, TLS 1.3 inside, Google 2012, IETF 2021) is introduced in ch10-modern-p6 and again in ch11-modern-p5 as if new, with no back-reference.
judge_fix: ch11-modern-p5: '*QUIC*, met in Chapter 10 (Section 05), replaces TCP entirely for HTTP traffic. What matters here: each stream is ordered independently, so a lost packet on stream A no longer holds back stream B. (RFC 9000, 2021; the name began as Quick UDP Internet Connections, but the standard treats it as just a name.) Google rolled it out to essentially all Chrome users by 2017, years before the IETF standard. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) is just HTTP semantics over QUIC. As of 2026 it carries roughly a third of web traffic by volume ...' Cut the repeated list of what QUIC rebuilds. Leave ch10-modern-p6 apart from the statistic (see 12).

quote: Receivers periodically advertise a window (how many more bytes they have buffer space to accept)
problem: The receive window is explained in Section 02 and again in Section 04, almost word for word ('senders never have more than that many in flight' and 'The sender never has more than that many bytes in flight'). The two passages also disagree: Section 02 says receivers advertise it 'periodically', while ch10-aimd-p2 and the Fig 10.4 caption say 'In every ACK'.
fix: ch10-why-p2: replace the sentence with 'The receiver's advertised *window* (Section 04) caps how many bytes may be in flight.'
reason: Section 02 says receivers advertise the window 'periodically'; ch10-aimd-p2 and the Fig 10.4 caption say 'in every ACK'. Small but a real inconsistency. Section 02 as the overview and 04 as the detail is acceptable.
judge_fix: ch10-why-p2: 'Receivers advertise a *window* in their acknowledgements (how many more bytes they have buffer space to accept), and senders never have more than that many in flight.'

quote: Part I closed inside a CPU. Part III leaves the CPU.
problem: The reader has just finished Part II, and the Part III tagline right above says 'Parts I and II built one machine… Part III steps off the motherboard.' The first line of the part then skips Part II entirely, which reads as if the reader had missed something.
fix: ch8-bridge-p1: 'Parts I and II stayed inside one machine. Part III leaves it.' The rest of the paragraph, which ties back to Chapter 1's transistor, can stay.
reason: The Part III tagline says Parts I and II built one machine; ch8-bridge-p1 then opens as if Part I were the last part read.
judge_fix: ch8-bridge-p1 opening: 'Parts I and II stayed inside one machine. Part III leaves it.' Keep the rest (the Chapter 1 transistor tie-back). Leave the section label alone.

quote: Every layer of the network stack, from here onward, exhibits the same arc
problem: Two consecutive chapter-closing insight strips make the same point. Ch10 says 'protocol invented for a reason; protocol exploited; protocol patched'. Ch11 says 'Every protocol in this chapter follows the same arc… none of these protocols was correctly designed at first issue.' The same lesson also closes ch8-ethernet-p11 and ch9-security-p2.
fix: Cut the last sentence of ch10-attacks-p9 ('Every layer of the network stack, from here onward, exhibits the same arc: …'), leaving it on 'State is the attack surface'. ch11-modern-p7 then makes the arc point once, with its examples.
reason: ch10-attacks-p9's last sentence announces the same protocol-invented-exploited-patched arc that ch11-modern-p7 then states as its whole point. Law 2: made once, in its strongest place.
judge_fix: ch10-attacks-p9: cut the last sentence ('Every layer of the network stack, from here onward, exhibits the same arc: ...'), ending on 'TLS (state cryptographically authenticated).'

quote: By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests
problem: QUIC/HTTP/3 usage is given twice, with different years and measures: 'well over a quarter of web requests' in 2024 (Ch10) and 'roughly a third of web traffic by volume' in 2026 (Ch11). The reader is left comparing two numbers for the same thing.
fix: Keep one figure. Cut 'By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests, and the share is growing.' from ch10-modern-p6 and leave the 2026 figure in ch11-modern-p5.
reason: QUIC adoption given twice with different years and measures (2024 requests vs 2026 traffic by volume).
judge_fix: ch10-modern-p6: cut 'By 2024 it carried well over a quarter of web requests, and the share is growing.' Keep the 2026 figure in ch11-modern-p5.

quote: Promises (standardised in ES6, the 2015 edition of the language's ECMAScript standard)
problem: Fig 12.2 has just taught the editions as ES3, ES5 and ES2015, and Fig 12.4 labels the same edition 'promises, ES2015'. This paragraph adds a third name, ES6, and explains ECMAScript again as if it were new.
fix: 'Promises (standardised in ES2015, Fig 12.2)'.
reason: Fig 12.2 and Fig 12.4 label the edition ES2015; ch12-loop-p4 introduces a third name, ES6, and re-explains ECMAScript.
judge_fix: ch12-loop-p4: 'Promises (standardised in ES2015, Fig 12.2)'.

quote: became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986
problem: The Morris worm is told again from scratch: Cornell student, aged 23, fingerd overflow, about ten percent of the internet, first conviction under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Chapter 3 opened its buffer-overflow section with the same story, and Ch9 gives no back-reference. The machine count also differs: 'about six thousand' in Ch3, 'between five thousand and ten thousand' here.
fix: In ch9-security-p2, introduce him as 'Robert Tappan Morris, the Cornell graduate student of Chapter 3, whose father…' and cut 'became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986' (Chapter 3 already says it). Keep the network-side material (re-infection, CERT).
reason: Ch9 retells the Morris worm from scratch (student, age, fingerd, ten percent, CFAA conviction) without referring to Chapter 3 and with a different machine count (about six thousand in Ch3; five to ten thousand here).
judge_fix: ch9-security-p2: 'Robert Tappan Morris, the Cornell graduate student of Chapter 3, whose father was the chief scientist at the NSA's National Computer Security Center, ...'; change the count to 'roughly six thousand machines (about ten percent of the internet of the time)'; replace 'Morris was traced within days and became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986.' with 'Morris was traced within days.' Keep the network side (re-infection, CERT).

quote: about twenty separate operations across four layers
problem: The 'four' are the four exchanges of Fig 11.3: DNS, TCP, TLS and HTTP. Under Chapter 8's model, DNS and HTTP (and arguably TLS) all sit in the single Application layer, so 'four layers' misuses a term the book defined.
fix: 'it performs about twenty separate operations in four exchanges, one after another, and the page appears only at the end.'
reason: ch11-http-p6 says 'four layers' but the four are the exchanges of Fig 11.3 (DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP), most of which are Application layer under Chapter 8's model.
judge_fix: ch11-http-p6: 'it performs about twenty separate operations in four exchanges, one after another, and the page appears only at the end.'

quote: Sixty parallel requests now share one connection
problem: Earlier in the same paragraph the page needs 'HTML, then 10 stylesheets, then 30 JavaScript files, then 50 images', which is 91 resources. The 'sixty' matches nothing.
fix: 'Every one of those requests now shares one connection, with no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.'
reason: The paragraph lists 1 + 10 + 30 + 50 = 91 resources, then says 'Sixty parallel requests'.
judge_fix: ch11-modern-p2: 'All of those requests now share one connection, with no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.'

quote: Wi-Fi runs around 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz; cellular at 700 MHz to several GHz
problem: In the same section, Fig 8.2 and its strip give Wi-Fi '2.4, 5 and 6 GHz' and cellular 'from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz'. Fig 8.7's strip then says '2.4 or 5 GHz'. That is three versions of the same bands.
fix: ch8-substrates-p4: 'Wi-Fi runs at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.' Fig 8.7 strip: 'such as 2.4, 5 or 6 GHz for Wi-Fi'.
reason: Three different band lists in one section: ch8-substrates-p4 (Wi-Fi 2.4 and 5 GHz; cellular 700 MHz to several GHz), Fig 8.2 (2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; below 1 GHz to tens of GHz), and the Fig 8.7 strip (2.4 or 5 GHz).
judge_fix: ch8-substrates-p4: 'Wi-Fi runs at 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz; cellular from below 1 GHz to tens of GHz; satellite up to tens of GHz.' Fig 8.7 strip: 'such as 2.4, 5 or 6 GHz for Wi-Fi'.

quote: The first standard Ethernet, 10BASE5 (10 Mbps over coaxial cable), used Manchester encoding
problem: Section 04 introduces Ethernet and 10BASE5 before Section 05 introduces Ethernet itself. Section 05 then introduces 10BASE5 again ('the standardised 10BASE5… over a single thick coaxial cable').
fix: ch8-encoding-p3: 'The first standard Ethernet (Section 05) used Manchester encoding because it could not afford to lose synchronisation on a long run of zeros.'
reason: ch8-encoding-p3 introduces Ethernet and 10BASE5 with speed and medium before Section 05, which introduces both again.
judge_fix: ch8-encoding-p3: 'The first standard Ethernet (Section 05) used Manchester encoding because it could not afford to lose synchronisation on a long run of zeros.'

quote: In switched Ethernet each link joins just two devices, so collisions no longer happen
problem: 'Switches ended collisions' is said three times in one section: p4 ('collisions stopped happening'), the Fig 8.8 strip 'Today', and the Fig 8.10 strip 'No more collisions'.
fix: Cut the Fig 8.10 strip bullet 'No more collisions'.
reason: 'Collisions stopped with switches' is said in ch8-ethernet-p4, the Fig 8.8 strip and the Fig 8.10 strip. The 8.10 bullet adds the full-duplex mechanism, so cut the 8.8 one rather than the 8.10 one.
judge_fix: Fig 8.8 strip 'Today': 'Wi-Fi uses the same random backoff but tries to avoid collisions rather than detect them.' Keep the Fig 8.10 bullet.

quote: The first 24 bits are an OUI, bought by a manufacturer from the IEEE
problem: The OUI split is explained three times: in p7 (with the B8:27:EB example), in the Fig 8.9 caption (with the same example) and in the strip bullet 'The halves'.
fix: Cut the Fig 8.9 strip bullet 'The halves'.
reason: The OUI split is in ch8-ethernet-p7, the Fig 8.9 caption (same example) and the strip bullet 'The halves', which adds nothing.
judge_fix: Cut the Fig 8.9 strip bullet 'The halves'.

quote: In practice the top three blur into the application
problem: Why TCP/IP folds OSI's layers is explained four times in one section: in p3, the Fig 8.11 caption, the Fig 8.12 caption and the Fig 8.12 strip bullet 'HTTP as an example'.
fix: Cut 'In practice the top three blur into the application, which is why the internet runs on the four layers of TCP/IP.' from the Fig 8.11 caption, and cut the Fig 8.12 strip bullet 'HTTP as an example'.
reason: Why TCP/IP folds the OSI layers is said in ch8-layers-p3, the Fig 8.11 caption, the Fig 8.12 caption and the Fig 8.12 strip bullet 'HTTP as an example'.
judge_fix: Fig 8.11 caption: cut 'In practice the top three blur into the application, which is why the internet runs on the four layers of TCP/IP.' Fig 8.12 strip: cut the bullet 'HTTP as an example'.

quote: IANA handed out its last blocks of IPv4 addresses on 3 February 2011
problem: The strip bullet 'The dates' repeats ch9-v6-p1 word for word ('at IANA's central pool on 3 February 2011, and at the regional registries over the years that followed'). The caption gives 2011 a third time.
fix: Cut the Fig 9.8 strip bullet 'The dates'.
reason: The Fig 9.8 strip bullet 'The dates' repeats ch9-v6-p1 almost word for word.
judge_fix: Cut the Fig 9.8 strip bullet 'The dates'.

quote: Twelve organisations run it as thirteen named servers
problem: The strip bullet 'The root' repeats ch11-dns-p3 almost verbatim: twelve organisations, thirteen servers a. to m.root-servers.net, anycast, over a thousand sites.
fix: Cut the Fig 11.5 strip bullet 'The root'.
reason: The Fig 11.5 strip bullet 'The root' repeats ch11-dns-p3 (twelve organisations, thirteen servers a to m, anycast, over a thousand sites).
judge_fix: Cut the Fig 11.5 strip bullet 'The root'.

quote: TLS 1.3 uses Diffie–Hellman key agreement: each side sends a public half and combines the other's
problem: The Fig 11.10 strip repeats AES's key sizes and CPU speed from p6 ('Symmetric'). It then repeats the Diffie–Hellman mechanics from p7 ('In TLS'), which Section 05 explains a third time in ch11-tls-p2.
fix: Cut the 'Symmetric' bullet. Replace 'In TLS' with: 'In TLS. Section 05 shows the exchange inside the handshake (Fig 11.11).'
reason: The Fig 11.10 strip 'Symmetric' bullet repeats ch11-crypto-p6, and 'In TLS' repeats the Diffie-Hellman mechanics of p7, which ch11-tls-p2 explains again.
judge_fix: Cut the 'Symmetric' bullet. Replace 'In TLS' with: 'In TLS. Section 05 shows the exchange inside the handshake (Fig 11.11).'

quote: The resolver caches the answer for the time to live (TTL) the authoritative server sets
problem: Chapter 9 taught TTL as the IP header's hop counter, which drops by one per router. Here the same acronym is a time in seconds, with no note that the meaning has changed.
fix: 'The resolver caches the answer for its time to live (TTL), a span of time set by the authoritative server, not the hop count of the IP header's TTL (Fig 9.4): typically 5 minutes to 24 hours.'
reason: Chapter 9 taught TTL as the IP header's hop counter; ch11-dns-p5 reuses the acronym for a time span with no note. The two meanings are easy to confuse.
judge_fix: ch11-dns-p5: 'The resolver caches the answer for its time to live (TTL), a span of time the authoritative server sets (typically 5 minutes to 24 hours), not the hop count of the IP header's TTL (Fig 9.4), and returns it to the laptop.'

quote: a keyed hash of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)
problem: The SYN cookie is built on a 'keyed hash' that is 'hard to forge without the server's secret key'. Cryptographic hashes are explained only in Chapter 11, Section 04.
fix: 'a keyed hash (a fingerprint of those values mixed with the server's secret key; Chapter 11, Section 04 explains hashes) of the (source IP, …)'.
reason: The SYN-cookie mechanism rests on a 'keyed hash', but 'hash' appears nowhere in Parts I and II and is explained only in Ch11 Section 04. This is main prose, not a strip.
judge_fix: ch10-attacks-p4: 'a keyed hash (a fixed-size scramble that only someone holding the server's secret key can compute; Chapter 11, Section 04) of the (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, time bucket)'.

quote: Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, brought into the Netscape-Sun partnership)
problem: In April or May 1995 the partnership already exists. Two paragraphs later, 'In December 1995 Netscape announced a partnership with Sun' and renamed the language. Which came first?
fix: ch12-eich-p1: 'Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, already in talks with Netscape over Java)'.
reason: ch12-eich-p1 puts Bill Joy inside a 'Netscape-Sun partnership' in April/May 1995, while ch12-eich-p3 has Netscape announce a partnership with Sun in December 1995. The apparent contradiction is real. Eich's foreword names Joy as an upper-management sponsor in May 1995 and a trademark license with Sun signed in early December 1995.
judge_fix: ch12-eich-p1: 'Bill Joy (Sun co-founder, one of the project's sponsors)'. ch12-eich-p3: 'In December 1995 Netscape signed a trademark license with Sun Microsystems and renamed it again, to *JavaScript*.' Source: Eich's foreword to Node Up and Running (safaribooksonline.com, node-up-and/9781449332235/pr03.html); webdevelopmenthistory.com/1995-the-birth-of-javascript/.

quote: everything else in the next five chapters is what we build on top of it
problem: Part III has five chapters, and this sentence is in the first of them. From here 'the next five' would run to Chapter 13, which is in Part IV.
fix: 'everything else in Part III is what we build on top of it.'
reason: ch8-bridge-p3 sits in the first chapter of a five-chapter part; 'the next five chapters' runs into Part IV.
judge_fix: ch8-bridge-p3: 'everything else in Part III is what we build on top of it.'

quote: generalising the linked-notes program he had already built for himself at CERN
problem: p2 introduces the same program a second time ('a little hypertext program Berners-Lee had written years earlier for himself, called ENQUIRE'). Similarly, p5's httpd, WorldWideWeb and first-page details reappear in the Fig 11.1 strip.
fix: p1: 'generalising ENQUIRE, the linked-notes program he had built for himself at CERN'. p2: replace the clause with 'design notes in Berners-Lee's own ENQUIRE'.
reason: ch11-bernerslee-p1 and p2, adjacent paragraphs, introduce the same CERN linked-notes program twice, the second time naming it ENQUIRE. The Fig 11.1 strip adds new detail, so leave it.
judge_fix: p1: 'generalising ENQUIRE, the linked-notes program he had built for himself at CERN.' p2: replace the clause with 'design notes in Berners-Lee's own ENQUIRE'.

quote: The first V8, in 2008, had no interpreter and compiled everything straight to machine code.
problem: This repeats ch12-node-p1 ('V8 began by compiling everything straight to machine code'). Likewise, the Fig 12.6 strip 'History' repeats ch12-node-p3's JSConf EU, November 2009.
fix: Cut that first sentence of the Fig 12.5 strip 'Then and now'. In Fig 12.6 'History', keep only 'libuv was written for Node in 2011, to bring it to Windows.'
reason: The Fig 12.5 strip 'Then and now' first sentence repeats ch12-node-p1. The Fig 12.6 strip 'History' repeats ch12-node-p3's JSConf EU, November 2009.
judge_fix: Fig 12.5 strip 'Then and now': 'SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore also run tiers of interpreters and compilers today.' Fig 12.6 strip 'History': 'libuv was written for Node in 2011, to bring it to Windows.'

quote: The policy arrived with JavaScript itself, in Netscape Navigator 2.0.
problem: ch12-security-p2 has just said the same thing: 'introduced in Netscape 2.0, the same release that shipped JavaScript itself'.
fix: Fig 12.8 strip 'History': keep only 'Cookies follow older, looser rules: they ignore the port, for one.'
reason: The Fig 12.8 strip 'History' first sentence repeats ch12-security-p2 almost verbatim.
judge_fix: Fig 12.8 strip 'History': 'Cookies follow older, looser rules: they ignore the port, for one.'
